title: Functional and Molecular Brain Imaging
summary: Understand how fMRI, diffusion imaging and PET reveal brain activity, wiring and drug targets in living people.

lessons.title: The BOLD Signal and Neurovascular Coupling

levels.kid:
Your brain is always busy, and busy brain cells need fuel. That fuel arrives in your blood, carried by red blood cells full of oxygen.

When one part of your brain works hard, like when you look at a picture, extra blood rushes to that spot. It is like a pizza shop sending too many pizzas to a party. More food arrives than the guests can eat!

Blood with lots of oxygen and blood with less oxygen act a little differently inside a giant magnet. A special machine called an **MRI scanner** can notice that difference. So scientists can watch which brain parts are busy, without any needles or surgery. They are not seeing the cells talk. They are seeing the blood that rushes in to help.
levels.hs:
**Functional MRI (fMRI)** lets scientists see which brain regions are active in living people. It does not measure electrical signals from neurons directly. Instead it measures the **BOLD signal**, which stands for **Blood Oxygen Level Dependent**.

Here is how it works:
- Hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. **Oxyhemoglobin** (carrying oxygen) is barely magnetic. **Deoxyhemoglobin** (oxygen released) is **paramagnetic**, meaning it disturbs the magnetic field around it.
- Deoxyhemoglobin makes the MRI signal from nearby tissue fade faster, so the image gets a little darker.
- When neurons become active, nearby blood vessels widen and blood flow rises a lot, more than the extra oxygen the cells use. This oversupply flushes out deoxyhemoglobin, so the MRI signal goes **up** by roughly 1 to 5 percent.

The link between neural activity and local blood flow is called **neurovascular coupling**.

A real example: if you watch a flickering checkerboard, the **visual cortex** at the back of your brain shows a BOLD increase. The response is slow. It starts a second or two after the stimulus, peaks around 5 to 6 seconds, and can dip below baseline afterward. This curve is called the **hemodynamic response function**. Because blood is slower than neurons, fMRI shows *where* activity happens well (millimeters) but *when* only roughly (seconds).
levels.college:
The BOLD contrast was described by **Seiji Ogawa** and colleagues in 1990, who showed that MRI images of rat brain changed with blood oxygenation. Human functional studies followed in 1992.

**Physics.** Deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic, creating microscopic field inhomogeneities around vessels. These speed up dephasing of proton spins, shortening **T2*** (and T2). BOLD fMRI uses **T2*-weighted gradient-echo EPI** sequences sensitive to this effect. Less deoxyhemoglobin means longer T2* and a brighter signal.

**Physiology.** BOLD reflects a balance of three variables:
- **CBF** (cerebral blood flow): rises sharply, often 30 to 70 percent with strong stimulation.
- **CMRO2** (oxygen metabolism): rises less, roughly 10 to 30 percent.
- **CBV** (cerebral blood volume): rises modestly, adding deoxyhemoglobin.

Because flow outpaces oxygen use, the **oxygen extraction fraction falls**, venous blood becomes more oxygenated, and BOLD signal rises. Fox and Raichle's PET work in the 1980s first reported this flow-metabolism mismatch.

**The hemodynamic response function (HRF).** It has a possible brief **initial dip**, a main positive peak about 4 to 6 seconds after onset, and a **post-stimulus undershoot** lasting tens of seconds. That undershoot is thought to reflect slow recovery of blood volume and lingering metabolism.

**Neurovascular coupling mechanisms.** Active synapses release glutamate, triggering vasoactive signals:
- **Nitric oxide** from neurons (via nNOS) relaxes vascular smooth muscle.
- **Prostaglandins** (e.g., PGE2) and **EETs**, partly via astrocytes.
- **Potassium** released during activity can dilate arterioles.
- **Pericytes** on capillaries may regulate capillary diameter.

The main point is that BOLD is an indirect, vascular signal. Coupling is driven largely by feedforward signals from synaptic activity, not by an oxygen deficit.
levels.phd:
The key study linking BOLD to neural activity is **Logothetis et al. (2001, Nature)**. They recorded simultaneously with fMRI and intracortical electrodes in macaque visual cortex. **Local field potentials (LFP)** predicted BOLD better than multi-unit spiking, especially when spiking adapted while LFP and BOLD persisted. The conclusion was that BOLD more closely reflects **synaptic input and local processing** than output spiking. This fits energy budgets (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001), in which postsynaptic currents and action potentials dominate signaling costs.

**Feedforward versus feedback.** Early models assumed flow rises to meet an energy deficit. Yet CBF increases far exceed what oxygen delivery requires (the **Buxton–Frank oxygen limitation model** explains part of this). Flow can also rise when blood oxygen or glucose is abundant. Most evidence supports **neurotransmitter-driven feedforward** signaling. Glutamate acts on NMDA receptors to drive nNOS and NO production. Interneuron subtypes contribute too: NOS-expressing and VIP interneurons promote dilation, and NPY and somatostatin interneurons can promote constriction. Astrocytic Ca2+ signaling through the COX/PGE2 and EET pathways has been proposed, but its timing is debated, since astrocytic Ca2+ often lags arteriolar dilation.

**Capillary versus arteriolar control.** Hall, Attwell and colleagues (2014) argued that pericytes dilate capillaries before arterioles and produce much of the flow increase. Others (Hill et al., 2015) found contractile control mainly in smooth-muscle-covered precapillary segments. Definitions of pericyte subtypes drive much of this dispute.

**Quantitative BOLD.** The **Davis model (1998)** uses hypercapnia calibration to estimate the relative change in CMRO2 from BOLD and ASL-measured CBF. It typically yields a CBF:CMRO2 coupling ratio of about 2 to 4. Because of **Grubb's relation** (CBV ∝ CBF^~0.38), volume effects must be modeled.

**Negative BOLD** occurs in regions adjacent to stimulated cortex. Shmuel et al. (2006) tied it to decreased neural activity, but vascular steal also contributes. The **initial dip** remains contested and is seen more reliably at high field and in optical imaging studies.
levels.expert:
For a clinician, the central fact is that BOLD reports vascular reactivity, so anything that changes vessels can masquerade as changes in neurons.

**Presurgical mapping pitfalls.** BOLD fMRI is used to localize motor and language cortex before resecting tumors or epileptic foci. It works best for **lateralizing language** and identifying motor hand knobs. It does not replace direct cortical stimulation for defining safe margins. A major hazard is **neurovascular uncoupling**. High-grade gliomas and AVMs disrupt autoregulation and alter vascular reactivity through tumor neovasculature and impaired smooth-muscle function. Real eloquent cortex near the lesion can then show **false-negative** activation. Breath-hold or CO2 **cerebrovascular reactivity mapping** can flag regions where absent BOLD is uninterpretable.

**Drug and physiological confounds.** For a pharmacology-minded reader, this is crucial. Agents that alter vessels or CO2 can change BOLD without changing neural activity. Examples include caffeine (an adenosine antagonist that constricts vessels and lowers baseline CBF), anesthetics, vasodilators and changes in arterial CO2. **Pharmacological MRI (phMRI)** must separate neural from vascular drug effects, often with CBF or calibrated measures.

**Population effects.** The hemodynamic response differs in neonates, aging, small-vessel disease, stroke and stroke penumbra. Comparing BOLD amplitude across groups therefore risks confusing vascular differences with neural differences.

**Spatial specificity.** Gradient-echo BOLD is weighted toward **draining veins**, so activity can be mislocalized millimeters downstream. At **7 T**, spin-echo sequences and **VASO** (vascular space occupancy) favor the microvasculature. These enable **laminar fMRI** that distinguishes feedforward input layers from feedback layers.

**Advances and open questions.** Fast fMRI has shown hemodynamic responses faster than once assumed. During sleep, slow neural waves are coupled to **CSF pulsations** (Fultz et al., 2019). Open questions include how vascular contributions vary by cell type and how to invert BOLD to infer neural activity in diseased brains.

keyPoints: BOLD = Blood Oxygen Level Dependent; fMRI measures blood, not spikes
Deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic and shortens T2*, darkening the signal
Blood flow rises more than oxygen use, so deoxyhemoglobin falls and signal rises
The hemodynamic response peaks about 5 seconds after activity
Neurovascular coupling uses NO, prostaglandins, K+, astrocytes and pericytes
BOLD tracks synaptic input (LFP) better than spiking; tumors can uncouple it

test.q: What does BOLD stand for?
test.explain: BOLD means Blood Oxygen Level Dependent contrast, the basis of most fMRI.

test.q: Which form of hemoglobin disturbs the local magnetic field?
test.explain: Deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic. It speeds signal decay, while oxyhemoglobin is barely magnetic.

test.q: Why does the BOLD signal increase in an active region?
choices: Flow rises more than oxygen use
Blood volume falls in nearby veins
test.explain: The large rise in flow washes out deoxyhemoglobin. Oxygen use rises far less, so the signal brightens.

test.q: About when does the main BOLD response peak after a brief stimulus?
test.explain: The hemodynamic response peaks around 4 to 6 seconds after onset, much slower than neural events.

test.q: fMRI is relatively strong at showing:
test.explain: Its spatial resolution is good, but its timing is limited by the slow blood response.

test.q: Which molecule made by neuronal nNOS relaxes vascular smooth muscle?
test.explain: Nitric oxide from nNOS diffuses to smooth muscle and causes dilation.

test.q: Which MRI parameter is shortened by deoxyhemoglobin and exploited by BOLD scans?
test.explain: BOLD fMRI uses T2*-weighted gradient-echo EPI, which is sensitive to field inhomogeneities caused by deoxyhemoglobin.

test.q: The dip below baseline after the BOLD peak is called the:
test.explain: The post-stimulus undershoot is the dip below baseline after the BOLD peak, and it lasts tens of seconds. The initial dip happens before the peak, not after.

test.q: Who first described BOLD contrast in 1990?
test.explain: Ogawa and colleagues described BOLD contrast in rat brain MRI in 1990.

test.q: What term describes the link between neural activity and local blood flow?
test.explain: Neurovascular coupling is how active neurons recruit more blood flow.

test.q: Deoxyhemoglobin is ___, meaning it distorts the magnetic field around it.
test.explain: Its unpaired electrons make it paramagnetic, which causes faster signal loss.

test.q: Contractile cells wrapped around capillaries that may regulate their diameter are called ___.
test.explain: Pericytes are proposed regulators of capillary blood flow.

kidTest.q: What does an MRI scanner notice to see busy brain parts?
kidTest.explain: It notices changes in the blood that rushes to busy areas.

kidTest.q: What carries oxygen in your blood?
kidTest.explain: Red blood cells carry oxygen.

kidTest.q: When a brain part works hard, how much blood arrives?
kidTest.explain: Extra blood arrives, like too many pizzas at a party.

kidTest.q: Which brain part gets busy when you look at a picture?
kidTest.explain: Looking at things uses the seeing part of the brain.

kidTest.q: The machine with a giant magnet is an M _ _ scanner.
kidTest.explain: An MRI scanner uses a big magnet to see inside the body.

advancedTest.q: In Logothetis et al. (2001), spiking adapted while BOLD persisted. The best interpretation is that BOLD:
choices: Is driven by glial heat production unrelated to neurons
Mainly reports output action potentials from pyramidal cells
Reflects synaptic input and local processing indexed by LFP
Reports oxygen deficit triggered by sustained firing
advancedTest.explain: LFP, which reflects synaptic and dendritic activity, tracked BOLD when spiking did not.

advancedTest.q: A glioma patient shows no motor BOLD activation next to the tumor, yet has normal strength. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Neurovascular uncoupling near the tumor causes a false negative
The scanner's T1 weighting was set too high for motor tasks
The draining veins are too large to show any activation
Motor function has moved to the opposite hemisphere
advancedTest.explain: Tumor-disrupted vascular reactivity can abolish BOLD despite intact neurons. CVR mapping helps detect this.

advancedTest.q: A drug lowers baseline cerebral blood flow by vasoconstriction but leaves neurons unchanged. A naive BOLD study could wrongly conclude:
choices: The hemodynamic response now peaks within milliseconds
Neural activity changed because the BOLD response changed
Deoxyhemoglobin stopped being paramagnetic after the drug
Oxygen use rose to equal the increase in blood flow
advancedTest.explain: BOLD reflects vascular state, so drug effects on vessels can masquerade as neural effects, as with caffeine.

advancedTest.q: Why is gradient-echo BOLD at standard field less suited to laminar fMRI than VASO?
choices: Its signal is weighted toward downstream draining veins
It is insensitive to small oxygen changes in gray matter
It measures CSF flow rather than blood flow
It depends on radiotracer binding in deep layers
advancedTest.explain: Pial and draining-vein weighting blurs signal across layers. VASO and spin-echo favor the microvasculature.

lessons.title: fMRI Experimental Design and Analysis: GLM and Multiple Comparisons

levels.kid:
Imagine you want to know which part of a big city lights up when a parade starts. You take a photo every two seconds. Some lights flicker for no reason, so one photo can fool you.

Scientists do something like this with a brain scanner called **fMRI**. A person in the scanner looks at pictures, then rests, then looks again, over and over. The computer checks every tiny spot of the brain. It asks: does this spot go up and down at the same times as the pictures?

There are thousands of spots, so a few will match just by luck. That's like flipping lots of coins and getting some lucky streaks. So scientists use extra-careful math rules to make sure a bright spot is real, not luck.
levels.hs:
**Functional MRI (fMRI)** measures the BOLD signal, a slow change in blood oxygen that follows brain activity. To find out which areas respond to a task, scientists need a smart **experimental design** and careful **statistics**.

Two common designs:
- **Block design**: the task is done for about 20-30 seconds, then rest, repeated. It gives strong signals.
- **Event-related design**: short, separate trials (like a single face flash) mixed in random order. It lets you study individual events, such as correct versus wrong answers.

The brain image is split into tiny 3D cubes called **voxels**, often about 2-3 mm wide. A typical scan has over 100,000 of them. For each voxel, scientists fit a **General Linear Model (GLM)**. This is a kind of regression that asks how well the predicted response to the task explains that voxel's signal over time.

That creates a big problem: **multiple comparisons**. If you run 100,000 tests at p < 0.05, about 5,000 voxels would look "active" by pure chance. Researchers correct for this with stricter thresholds.

A famous real example: in 2009, Craig Bennett scanned a **dead salmon** shown photos of people. Without correction, some voxels in the fish's brain looked "active." It was a joke with a serious point: uncorrected statistics produce false positives.
levels.college:
fMRI analysis treats each voxel's time series as data to be explained by a model of the experiment.

**Design choices**
- **Block designs** maximize detection power because sustained activity sums up in the BOLD response.
- **Event-related designs** with **jittered** intervals between trials let overlapping responses be separated. They also support trial sorting, such as remembered versus forgotten items.
- **Contrasts** compare conditions (faces > houses). This follows the logic of **subtraction**, which assumes the conditions differ in only one cognitive process.

**The GLM**: Y = Xβ + ε
- Y is the voxel time series. X is the **design matrix**: each column is a stimulus timing function **convolved with the hemodynamic response function (HRF)**, which peaks about 5-6 s after the event.
- **Nuisance regressors** handle unwanted signal: head-motion parameters, slow drifts (removed with a high-pass filter), and sometimes physiological noise.
- β estimates are fit by least squares. A contrast vector c gives a t statistic, cβ divided by its standard error, which produces a **statistical parametric map**.

**Preprocessing** usually comes first: motion correction, slice-timing correction, spatial normalization to a template (MNI space), and smoothing.

**Two-level (group) analysis**: subject-level contrast images feed a second-level model. This treats subjects as random effects, so the results generalize to the population.

**Multiple comparisons**
- **Bonferroni** divides α by the number of tests. This is too conservative because neighboring voxels are correlated.
- **Family-wise error (FWE)** control uses random field theory or permutation testing.
- **False discovery rate (FDR)** limits the expected *proportion* of false positives among the voxels declared active.
- **Cluster-level inference** first sets a voxel-level "cluster-forming" threshold, then tests whether clusters are larger than expected by chance.
levels.phd:
The GLM's validity rests on assumptions that are often violated.

**Temporal autocorrelation.** fMRI noise is serially correlated, so ordinary least squares underestimates variance and inflates t values. SPM uses an AR(1)+white-noise model with ReML estimation and **prewhitening**. FSL's FILM uses Tukey-tapered autocorrelation estimates. Under-modeling autocorrelation is worst at short TRs, a growing concern with multiband acquisitions (TR under 1 s).

**HRF variability.** A canonical double-gamma HRF misfits many regions and subjects; peak latency can vary by about ±1-2 s. Adding **temporal and dispersion derivatives**, or using finite impulse response (FIR) basis sets, captures this variability at the cost of degrees of freedom and harder inference (F tests).

**Design efficiency.** Efficiency, which scales as 1/(c(XᵀX)⁻¹cᵀ), depends on the contrast. Short, randomized designs favor detecting differences between conditions. Long blocks risk losing signal to the high-pass filter. Collinear regressors inflate variance in the β estimates, so Dale's work on optimal jittering and m-sequence designs addresses this.

**Inference controversies.** Eklund, Nichols and Knutsson (PNAS 2016) ran null analyses on resting-state data. Parametric cluster-wise inference at a lenient cluster-forming threshold (p = 0.01) gave familywise false-positive rates up to about 70%, against a nominal 5%. The cause was non-Gaussian spatial autocorrelation with heavier tails than random field theory assumes. Voxel-wise FWE was conservative, and nonparametric **permutation** testing held nominal rates. A bug in AFNI's 3dClustSim was also found and fixed. The headline claim that "40,000 studies are invalid" was overstated, but it shifted the field toward a cluster-forming threshold of p = 0.001, permutation methods, and **threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE)** (Smith & Nichols 2009).

**Circularity.** Vul et al. (2009) and Kriegeskorte et al. (2009) showed that choosing voxels by a test, then reporting effect sizes from the same data, inflates correlations ("double dipping"). Independent localizers or cross-validation avoid this.

**Reproducibility.** The NARPS study (Botvinik-Nezer et al., Nature 2020) had 70 teams analyze one dataset. Their conclusions about the same hypotheses varied widely, showing that the analysis pipeline itself is a major source of variance.
levels.expert:
For clinicians, task-fMRI GLM methods matter most in **presurgical mapping** of language and motor cortex near tumors, vascular malformations and epileptogenic lesions. Group-level logic does not transfer to single patients.

**Single-subject pitfalls**
- **Threshold dependence.** Language maps grow or vanish as the t threshold changes. Experienced centers review maps at several thresholds rather than one corrected cutoff. Many treat fMRI as a guide for **direct cortical stimulation (DCS)**, the reference standard, not a replacement for it. Reported sensitivity and specificity against DCS vary widely, roughly 60-100%.
- **Neurovascular uncoupling.** High-grade gliomas and AVMs can disrupt cerebrovascular reactivity, producing **false-negative** BOLD activity next to the lesion. This is dangerous because absent activation may be misread as safe-to-resect tissue. Breath-hold cerebrovascular reactivity mapping can flag affected regions.
- **Task compliance and motion.** Aphasic or paretic patients perform poorly. Movement correlated with the task, such as jaw motion in overt speech, creates activation-like artifacts that motion regressors cannot fully remove. Covert tasks and real-time quality monitoring help.
- **Laterality indices** for language dominance are moderately concordant with the Wada test. They are also sensitive to threshold, ROI and task (for example, verb generation versus semantic decision). Combining several tasks improves reliability.
- **Distortion.** EPI susceptibility distortion near air-tissue boundaries and resection cavities can shift activations by millimeters during coregistration to the neuronavigation scan. Field-map or reversed phase-encoding correction is recommended.

**Research frontiers**
- **Multivariate pattern analysis** and encoding models move beyond the voxel-wise GLM. They need cross-validated inference and permutation baselines.
- **Preregistration**, BIDS formatting and containerized pipelines (fMRIPrep) address analytic flexibility.
- Marek et al. (Nature 2022) showed brain-wide association effects are small, often requiring thousands of participants. Within-subject, densely sampled designs are a complementary answer.
- Laminar fMRI at 7T applies GLMs at the scale of cortical layers, but draining-vein bias toward the pial surface remains unsolved.

An open question is how to report single-patient uncertainty. Bayesian posterior probability maps and test-retest confidence intervals are promising but not yet standard practice.

keyPoints: Block designs maximize power; jittered event-related designs isolate single trials
The GLM models each voxel as Y = Xβ + ε with HRF-convolved regressors
Contrasts like faces > houses produce statistical maps via t tests
Testing ~100,000 voxels demands multiple-comparison correction (FWE, FDR, cluster)
Eklund 2016 showed lenient parametric cluster inference inflates false positives
Clinical fMRI maps depend on threshold and can miss activity near tumors

test.q: Why do researchers convolve stimulus timings with the hemodynamic response function?
choices: To correct for multiple statistical tests
To convert voxels into standard MNI space
To model the delayed, slow BOLD response
To remove head-motion artifacts from data
test.explain: BOLD peaks about 5-6 s after an event. Convolution with the HRF turns event timings into the expected signal shape.

test.q: What is the main advantage of a block design over an event-related design?
choices: No need for any rest periods
test.explain: Sustained activity sums in the BOLD response, giving strong detection power. Event-related designs are better for analyzing individual trials.

test.q: In Y = Xβ + ε, what does X represent?
choices: The residual noise in each scan
The fitted effect sizes per voxel
test.explain: X is the design matrix, whose columns are the modeled task and nuisance regressors. Y is the data and β the estimates.

test.q: Running 100,000 voxel tests at p < 0.05 with no correction would yield roughly how many false positives under the null?
test.explain: 5% of 100,000 tests is about 5,000 chance 'activations.'

test.q: What did the dead salmon study demonstrate?
choices: Fish brains respond to human faces
Block designs fail in small animals
test.explain: Voxels in a dead fish looked 'active' without multiple-comparison correction, a vivid demonstration of false positives.

test.q: Why is Bonferroni correction considered too conservative for fMRI?
choices: It ignores the number of tests
It controls the false discovery rate
It applies at the subject level alone
test.explain: Bonferroni treats tests as independent, but nearby voxels share signal, so the effective number of tests is smaller.

test.q: False discovery rate (FDR) correction controls:
choices: The expected share of false positives among hits
The chance of even one false positive
The size of clusters formed by thresholding
test.explain: FDR limits the proportion of declared-active voxels that are false. FWE controls the probability of even one false positive.

test.q: Why are head-motion parameters added to the GLM?
test.explain: Motion regressors soak up unwanted signal so it isn't mistaken for task activity.

test.q: Treating subjects as random effects in a second-level analysis allows conclusions about:
test.explain: Random-effects group models account for between-subject variability, so results generalize to the population.

test.q: What is the name for a tiny 3D cube of brain image data, often 2-3 mm wide?
test.explain: A voxel is a volume element, the 3D counterpart of a pixel.

test.q: Varying the time between trials in event-related designs is called ___ and helps separate overlapping responses.
test.explain: Jittered intervals make overlapping BOLD responses separable in the GLM.

test.q: What does GLM stand for?
test.explain: The General Linear Model is the regression framework used for voxel-wise fMRI analysis.

kidTest.q: What does an fMRI scanner help scientists see?
choices: How tall a person will grow
What a person ate for lunch
kidTest.explain: fMRI shows which brain areas are working during a task.

kidTest.q: Why do scientists use extra-careful math?
choices: So the pictures look more colorful
So the scanner gets less noisy
kidTest.explain: With thousands of spots, some match by luck. Careful math stops these fake results from being counted.

kidTest.q: What does the person in the scanner often do?
choices: Sleep the whole time with no task
Run around the room very fast
Do a task, then rest, then repeat
kidTest.explain: Switching between a task and rest helps show which spots follow the task.

kidTest.q: Flipping lots of coins is like checking many brain spots because:
choices: Coins are found in the brain
The coins land on heads more
Some will look special by luck
kidTest.explain: With many tries, a few lucky streaks happen just by chance.

kidTest.q: A scientist scanned a dead fish to show a math mistake. What fish? s _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: The dead salmon looked 'active' when the careful math wasn't used.

advancedTest.q: Eklund et al. (2016) found inflated false positives mainly for parametric cluster inference at lenient thresholds because:
choices: Spatial autocorrelation had heavier tails than random field theory assumes
Voxel-wise FWE thresholds were set far too liberally across packages
Resting-state data contained hidden task signals in most subjects
Permutation tests underestimated the null distribution of cluster sizes
advancedTest.explain: Non-Gaussian spatial autocorrelation violated RFT assumptions. Permutation testing held nominal error rates, and voxel-wise FWE was conservative.

advancedTest.q: A lab selects voxels where activity correlates with anxiety, then reports r = 0.85 from those same voxels. The main flaw is:
choices: Using an FIR basis set without F tests
Circular analysis inflating the effect size
advancedTest.explain: Selecting and estimating on the same data (double dipping) biases the effect upward. Independent data or cross-validation fixes it.

advancedTest.q: Near a high-grade glioma, a motor task shows no BOLD activation. The safest interpretation is:
choices: Stricter FDR correction would reveal the true map
Uncoupling may hide real function, so verify with DCS
The cortex is non-eloquent and safe to resect
The HRF peaked early, so the GLM caught it fully
advancedTest.explain: Tumors can disrupt neurovascular coupling and cause false negatives. Direct cortical stimulation remains the reference standard.

advancedTest.q: Under-modeled temporal autocorrelation in a first-level GLM most directly causes:
choices: Loss of signal to the high-pass filter
Underestimated variance and inflated t values
advancedTest.explain: Serially correlated noise means fewer effective degrees of freedom. Ignoring it shrinks standard errors and inflates t statistics, which is why prewhitening is used.

lessons.title: Resting-State fMRI and Functional Connectivity

levels.kid:
Even when you lie still with your eyes closed, your brain is busy. It never really switches off.

Scientists can watch this with a big magnet machine called an MRI scanner. It sees where blood flows in the brain. Blood flow rises and falls slowly, like gentle waves.

Here is the cool part. Brain areas that work as a team rise and fall **together**, like friends humming the same song in different rooms. Scientists call these teams **networks**.

One famous team is the **default mode network**. It gets busy when you daydream or think about yourself. It gets quieter when you focus on a hard puzzle.

Brain surgeons can use these maps to find important areas, like the ones for moving, before an operation.
levels.hs:
Most fMRI studies give people a task, like tapping a finger, and look for brain areas whose signal goes up. **Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI)** does something different: the person simply lies in the scanner, usually for about 5 to 15 minutes, doing nothing in particular.

The **BOLD signal** (blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal) still drifts up and down on its own, mostly in slow waves below about 0.1 Hz, roughly one cycle every 10 seconds or more. In 1995, **Bharat Biswal** noticed that the left and right motor areas fluctuated in sync even when people were not moving.

This is measured as **functional connectivity**: the correlation between the signals of two brain regions over time. A high correlation means the regions tend to rise and fall together. It does not prove a direct wire between them.

Researchers have found a set of reliable **resting-state networks**:
- **Default mode network (DMN)**: active in mind-wandering and memory, quieter during focused tasks
- **Sensorimotor network**: movement and touch areas
- **Visual network**
- **Salience network**: notices important events
- **Frontoparietal control network**: attention and problem-solving

A real example: before removing a brain tumor, some hospitals use rs-fMRI to map motor and language networks in patients who cannot perform tasks well in the scanner.
levels.college:
Resting-state fMRI measures **spontaneous low-frequency BOLD fluctuations**, typically 0.01–0.1 Hz, while subjects rest without a task. Because these fluctuations are coordinated across distant regions, they reveal the brain's large-scale functional organization.

**Discovery.** Biswal and colleagues (1995) placed a seed in left motor cortex and found strong correlations with right motor cortex, the supplementary motor area and other motor regions at rest. Raichle and colleagues (2001) described a **default mode** of brain function: medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate/precuneus, inferior parietal lobule and medial temporal lobe that *deactivate* during goal-directed tasks.

**Main analysis approaches:**
- **Seed-based correlation**: extract the time series from a region of interest and correlate it with every voxel. Simple and easy to interpret, but depends on where you place the seed.
- **Independent component analysis (ICA)**: a data-driven method that separates the signal into spatially independent components. Some are networks; others are noise like head motion or vessels.
- **Graph theory**: treat regions as **nodes** and correlations as **edges**, then calculate properties such as hub strength, modularity and small-world organization.

**Preprocessing matters.** BOLD is contaminated by head motion, breathing and heartbeat. Pipelines therefore include motion correction, nuisance regression (motion parameters, white matter and CSF signals) and band-pass filtering. Tools such as **fMRIPrep** standardize these steps.

**Key interpretive caution:** functional connectivity is a statistical dependence, not anatomy. Two regions can correlate because they share input from a third region. Anatomical wiring is studied with other methods. Also, correlation says nothing about direction (A to B vs B to A).

**Anticorrelation.** The DMN tends to be negatively correlated with task-positive attention networks. That finding depends partly on preprocessing choices, discussed further at deeper levels.
levels.phd:
**Physiological basis.** Resting BOLD fluctuations track slow changes in neural activity. Simultaneous recordings in primates and humans link them to the slow envelope of gamma-band local field potential power and to infraslow (<0.1 Hz) electrical activity. Studies under anesthesia, sleep and in disconnection patients show that interhemispheric connectivity depends heavily on the **corpus callosum** but can partly persist through subcortical routes. Structural connectivity therefore constrains functional connectivity but does not determine it; indirect polysynaptic paths and shared modulatory input (for example arousal systems) shape correlations.

**The global signal controversy.** **Global signal regression (GSR)** removes the mean whole-brain time series, which cleans up motion and respiratory artifacts. Murphy and colleagues (2009) showed mathematically that GSR forces the distribution of correlations to center near zero, so it can *create* anticorrelations. Fox and colleagues argued that DMN/task-positive anticorrelations survive without GSR, though they are weaker. The global signal itself correlates with vigilance and arousal, so it is partly neural and not pure noise.

**Motion artifact.** Power, Van Dijk and Satterthwaite (2012) showed that sub-millimeter head motion inflates short-distance and reduces long-distance correlations. That distortion produced spurious group differences, such as apparent developmental or autism effects. Remedies include frame censoring ('scrubbing') based on framewise displacement, ICA-AROMA, aCompCor and multi-echo denoising. None removes the artifact perfectly.

**Parcellation and individuality.** Yeo and colleagues (2011) defined 7- and 17-network atlases from 1,000 subjects. Glasser and colleagues (2016) produced a 360-area multimodal parcellation from the Human Connectome Project. Precision functional mapping, using hours of data per person (the Midnight Scan Club), shows that individual network topography differs substantially from group atlases. **Connectome fingerprinting** (Finn, 2015) can identify individuals from their connectivity profiles.

**Dynamics.** Sliding-window 'dynamic connectivity' suggests recurring brain states. However, sampling variability, motion and arousal changes can mimic these dynamics, so their neural significance remains disputed. Effective connectivity methods such as dynamic causal modeling try to estimate directed influences, but they rest on strong model assumptions.
levels.expert:
**Presurgical mapping.** Task fMRI fails when patients are aphasic, paretic, sedated, young or cognitively impaired. Rs-fMRI needs no cooperation beyond staying still, and it can even be acquired under anesthesia, which preserves sensorimotor networks reasonably well. Work at Washington University (Leuthardt, Shimony and colleagues) used a multilayer perceptron trained on normative data to classify voxels into networks for individual tumor and epilepsy patients. They validated sensorimotor maps against intraoperative **direct cortical stimulation**. Language mapping is less reliable: lateralization agreement with Wada testing and stimulation is moderate, and the language network borders the frontoparietal control network. Rs-fMRI is therefore an adjunct to stimulation mapping, not a replacement.

**Pitfalls near lesions:**
- **Neurovascular uncoupling.** High-grade gliomas and arteriovenous malformations disturb the coupling between neural activity and blood flow. This can silence BOLD in cortex that still works, producing false negatives exactly where resection decisions are made. Breath-hold cerebrovascular reactivity maps help flag at-risk zones.
- **Mass effect and distortion.** Displaced anatomy and susceptibility artifact near resection cavities or blood products break atlas-based assumptions, so individual-level methods are needed.
- **Reliability.** Short scans of about 6 minutes give noisy edges; test-retest reliability of individual edges is often poor. Multi-echo acquisition and longer or concatenated runs help.

**Network neurosurgery and neuromodulation.** **Lesion network mapping** (Fox and colleagues) projects lesion locations onto a normative connectome. Lesions that cause the same symptom, such as hallucinations or criminality-associated behavior, often map to a shared network even when they sit in different places. Connectivity guides targets: subgenual cingulate anticorrelation predicts better TMS outcomes in depression and underlies the SAINT protocol. Connectivity of deep brain stimulation volumes predicts outcome in Parkinson disease and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

**Biomarkers and open questions.** Brain-wide association studies (Marek and colleagues, 2022) showed that brain-behavior correlations need thousands of subjects to replicate. That undercuts many small clinical connectivity 'biomarkers.' Still open: what neural process the infraslow signal actually reflects, whether network breakdown causes symptoms or results from them, and how to separate arousal effects from cognitive ones. Pharmacological rs-fMRI is growing, comparing drug and placebo connectivity profiles, but vascular drug effects can confound interpretation.

keyPoints: Resting-state fMRI records spontaneous slow BOLD fluctuations (about 0.01–0.1 Hz) without a task
Functional connectivity is the temporal correlation between regions, not proof of direct wiring
Biswal (1995) found synchronized motor cortex at rest; Raichle described the default mode network
Analyses: seed-based correlation, ICA and graph theory
Head motion and global signal regression can create spurious correlations
Rs-fMRI aids presurgical mapping but does not replace direct cortical stimulation

test.q: What does a resting-state fMRI scan ask the participant to do?
choices: Tap a finger in timed blocks
Lie still without a specific task
Name pictures shown on a screen
test.explain: Rs-fMRI records spontaneous activity while the person rests. Finger tapping and picture naming are task fMRI paradigms.

test.q: Functional connectivity between two regions is usually measured as the:
choices: Number of synapses linking the areas
Peak BOLD response to a stimulus
Thickness of the white matter tracts
Correlation of their signals over time
test.explain: Functional connectivity is a statistical dependence, typically a correlation, between two regions' BOLD time series.

test.q: In what frequency range are resting BOLD fluctuations mainly found?
test.explain: Resting BOLD fluctuations are infraslow, below about 0.1 Hz. The other ranges correspond to EEG rhythms.

test.q: Biswal's 1995 discovery showed that at rest:
choices: The frontal lobes were fully inactive
Blood flow in the brain became constant
The visual cortex stopped producing signal
Left and right motor cortex fluctuated together
test.explain: Biswal found that bilateral motor regions stayed correlated even without movement, which launched the rs-fMRI field.

test.q: Which network becomes less active during focused, goal-directed tasks?
test.explain: The default mode network deactivates during demanding external tasks and is engaged in mind-wandering and self-referential thought.

test.q: A key weakness of seed-based correlation analysis is that:
choices: Results depend on where the seed is placed
It requires a task to be performed
It works on structural images alone
It ignores the time course of signals
test.explain: Seed-based maps reflect the chosen region of interest. ICA is data-driven and avoids this choice.

test.q: Why does a strong correlation between two regions not prove a direct connection?
choices: Correlations are too weak to interpret
BOLD signal does not come from the brain
Correlations reflect white matter, not gray matter
Both regions may share input from a third area
test.explain: Shared input or indirect paths can make two regions correlate without a direct anatomical link.

test.q: Small head movements during scanning tend to:
test.explain: Motion inflates short-range and reduces long-range correlations, which can create false group differences.

test.q: In graph theory analyses of brain networks, brain regions are treated as:
test.explain: Regions are nodes and the connections between them are edges.

test.q: The data-driven method that separates rs-fMRI data into independent spatial components is called independent component ___.
test.explain: ICA separates networks from noise components without needing a seed.

test.q: What abbreviation names the network active during daydreaming, centered on the posterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex?
test.explain: The default mode network (DMN) includes the posterior cingulate/precuneus, medial prefrontal cortex and inferior parietal regions.

test.q: Removing the mean whole-brain signal is called global signal ___.
test.explain: Global signal regression (GSR) cleans artifacts but can artificially create anticorrelations.

kidTest.q: What does your brain do when you rest?
kidTest.explain: Your brain keeps working even when you rest.

kidTest.q: How do brain areas on the same team act?
kidTest.explain: Teammate areas go up and down together, like friends humming the same song.

kidTest.q: When is the default mode network busy?
kidTest.explain: It gets busy when you daydream or think about yourself.

kidTest.q: What does the MRI scanner watch in the brain?
kidTest.explain: The scanner sees changes in blood flow.

kidTest.q: Brain areas working as a team form a n _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Teams of brain areas that rise and fall together are called networks.

advancedTest.q: A study reports stronger DMN/attention-network anticorrelation after global signal regression. The best interpretation is:
choices: GSR removes motion, so the anticorrelation reflects direct inhibition
GSR centers correlations near zero, so part of the effect may be artifact
GSR reveals anticorrelations that are hidden by noise and are purely neural
GSR leaves correlation values unchanged, so the result is robust
advancedTest.explain: Murphy et al. (2009) showed that GSR mathematically forces seed correlations to sum to a negative value. This shifts the distribution so it centers near zero, which can create or exaggerate anticorrelations. Weaker DMN/task-positive anticorrelations do persist without GSR (e.g., Fox et al. 2009; Chang & Glover 2009), so the effect is likely partly real and partly artifact.

advancedTest.q: A patient group shows higher short-range and lower long-range connectivity than controls, and the patients moved more in the scanner. What is the most cautious conclusion?
choices: Short-range hubs compensate for the disease
The disease reorganizes cortex toward local wiring
Long tracts in patients have degenerated
Motion alone could produce this pattern
advancedTest.explain: Power and colleagues showed that motion produces exactly this distance-dependent pattern, so motion must be controlled before attributing it to disease.

advancedTest.q: In a high-grade glioma, rs-fMRI shows no motor network signal next to the tumor, yet stimulation evokes movement there. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Stimulation spreading current to distant cortex
Anesthesia suppressing the motor network itself
The motor network moving to the other hemisphere
Neurovascular uncoupling suppressing the BOLD signal
advancedTest.explain: Tumors can disturb neurovascular coupling, silencing BOLD in functioning cortex. Anesthesia preserves sensorimotor networks reasonably well, so it is a less likely cause; this false negative is why stimulation mapping remains the reference standard.

advancedTest.q: Why did brain-wide association studies (Marek, 2022) cast doubt on many small connectivity biomarker studies?
choices: Connectivity was shown to carry no individual information
Brain-behavior effects are small and need thousands of subjects
Larger scanners produced conflicting network atlases
Resting networks were found to vary randomly across scans
advancedTest.explain: True brain-behavior correlations are small, so small samples inflate and fail to replicate them. Fingerprinting shows that connectivity does carry individual information.

lessons.title: Diffusion MRI and Tractography for Surgical Planning

levels.kid:
Your brain has billions of tiny wires. They carry messages from one part to another. These wires are bundled together like the cables behind a TV.

Scientists found a clever trick to see these bundles without opening the head. Water inside the brain is always jiggling around. Inside a wire bundle, water can zoom along the wire easily, like cars on a highway. But it bumps into the sides if it tries to go across.

A special MRI scanner can tell which way the water likes to move. A computer then draws colorful lines showing where the wire bundles go.

Brain surgeons look at these maps before an operation. They plan a path that avoids important wires, like the ones that help you move or talk.
levels.hs:
**Diffusion MRI** is a type of brain scan that measures how water molecules move. Water molecules constantly wander randomly, a process called **diffusion**. In fluid-filled spaces, water spreads equally in every direction. This is called **isotropic** diffusion. In the brain's **white matter**, though, nerve fibers (axons) are packed into parallel bundles wrapped in fatty **myelin**. Water moves much more easily along the fibers than across them. This direction-dependent movement is called **anisotropic** diffusion.

By measuring diffusion in many directions, the scanner can estimate the main direction of the fibers in each small cube of brain, called a **voxel**. A number called **fractional anisotropy (FA)** runs from 0 (no preferred direction) to 1 (strongly one direction).

**Tractography** is a computer method that links these directions from voxel to voxel. The result is a 3D map of likely nerve pathways, called **tracts**. In the classic color code, red means left-right, green means front-back and blue means up-down.

Real example: before removing a tumor near the motor cortex, a neurosurgeon may map the **corticospinal tract**, the pathway that controls voluntary movement. The map is loaded into the surgical navigation system. This helps the surgeon remove as much tumor as possible while avoiding the tract, which lowers the risk of paralysis.
levels.college:
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) adds strong, paired **diffusion-sensing gradients** to an MRI sequence, usually a spin-echo echo-planar sequence (Stejskal-Tanner design). Stationary spins are dephased and then rephased. Spins that move along the gradient direction do not fully rephase, so they lose signal. The amount of signal loss follows S = S0·exp(−b·D). Here **b** (s/mm²) sums up gradient strength and timing. **D** is the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) along that direction.

**Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)** models diffusion in each voxel as a 3D ellipsoid, described by a symmetric 3×3 tensor. Measuring it needs at least 6 gradient directions plus a b=0 image. Clinical protocols usually use 30 or more. Diagonalizing the tensor gives three eigenvalues (λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ3) and their eigenvectors:
- **Principal eigenvector**: the estimated fiber orientation.
- **Mean diffusivity (MD)**: the average of the three eigenvalues.
- **Axial diffusivity (λ1)** and **radial diffusivity** (the average of λ2 and λ3).
- **FA**: the normalized spread of the eigenvalues.

**Deterministic tractography** (for example, FACT, Mori 1999) starts from seed regions and steps along the principal eigenvector. It stops when FA drops below a threshold (often about 0.15-0.2) or the path turns too sharply. **Probabilistic tractography** (for example, FSL's probtrackx) samples a distribution of possible orientations. It produces maps showing how likely each voxel is to be connected.

Common surgical targets:
- **Corticospinal tract**: movement.
- **Arcuate fasciculus / superior longitudinal fasciculus**: language, especially repetition.
- **Optic radiation and Meyer's loop**: vision. Meyer's loop is at risk in temporal lobectomy.

A classic limitation is **crossing fibers**. One tensor can show only one direction. Yet a large share of white-matter voxels (estimated at up to about 90% at typical resolution) contain several fiber populations. This can cause false tracts or missing tracts.

Separately, a bright DWI signal with low ADC marks the restricted diffusion of acute ischemic stroke. This is the most important everyday clinical use of DWI.
levels.phd:
The physical basis is the Einstein relation: mean squared displacement equals 2Dt in one dimension. With a diffusion time of tens of milliseconds and brain D ≈ 0.7-1.0 ×10⁻³ mm²/s, water travels roughly 10 µm. That is the scale of axons and glia, so diffusion MRI probes microstructure far below voxel resolution (about 2 mm). Anisotropy arises mainly from axonal membranes. Myelin adds to it but is not required: Beaulieu showed anisotropy in non-myelinated garfish olfactory nerve. So FA is not a myelin measure. Basser, Mattiello and LeBihan formalized DTI in 1994.

FA is sensitive but nonspecific. It falls with demyelination, axonal loss, edema, more crossing fibers, or partial volume with cerebrospinal fluid. Song and colleagues' shiverer and ischemia mouse work suggested radial diffusivity tracks myelin and axial diffusivity tracks axonal injury. However, this split fails in voxels with crossing fibers.

Models beyond the tensor address its limits:
- **High angular resolution diffusion imaging (HARDI)** with **constrained spherical deconvolution** (Tournier; MRtrix) estimates a fiber orientation distribution, resolving crossings.
- **Q-ball, diffusion spectrum imaging** and multi-shell sampling.
- **Diffusion kurtosis imaging** captures non-Gaussian diffusion.
- Biophysical compartment models such as **NODDI** (Zhang 2012) estimate neurite density and orientation dispersion. They rest on fixed-diffusivity assumptions that are now debated.

Tractography's central weakness is validity. In the ISMRM 2015 tractography challenge (Maier-Hein et al., 2017), most algorithms recovered most true bundles. Yet they also produced many more false bundles than true ones, largely at bottlenecks where tracts converge. Thomas et al. (2014) showed with macaque tracer comparisons that no parameter setting maximized both sensitivity and specificity. Tractography also cannot tell a fiber's direction (afferent from efferent) or detect synapses. Streamline counts are not a quantitative measure of connection strength. Methods such as SIFT/COMMIT try to make them more biologically meaningful.

Acquisition artifacts also matter. Echo-planar susceptibility distortion is corrected with reversed phase-encoding (FSL topup). Eddy currents and head motion need correction as well (eddy).
levels.expert:
In neuro-oncology, the clinical case for DTI-guided resection rests mainly on Wu et al. (2007, Neurosurgery). In a randomized trial of 238 patients with gliomas involving the pyramidal tract, functional neuronavigation improved the extent of resection in high-grade gliomas. It also improved postoperative motor outcomes and survival. Tractography is now routine for lesions near the corticospinal tract, the arcuate fasciculus or the optic radiation. It is integrated with navigation platforms (Brainlab, Medtronic StealthStation) and is CPT-reimbursable in the US.

Key pitfalls for the operating surgeon:
- **Brain shift.** After dural opening, cerebrospinal fluid loss and resection can move tracts by up to about 1 cm or more. Preoperative tracts drift out of registration as surgery proceeds. Intraoperative MRI updates or ultrasound-based correction help.
- **Peritumoral edema** lowers FA. With standard thresholds, tracts may falsely stop at the tumor edge, suggesting a tract is destroyed when it is only displaced or infiltrated. Free-water elimination and constrained spherical deconvolution reduce these false negatives.
- **Tract width is threshold-dependent.** A rendered tract is a model output, not an anatomical boundary. Groups typically keep a safety margin of about 5 mm. Subcortical stimulation studies (for example, Ostry, Berman, Kinoshita) correlate the motor-evoked-potential threshold with distance to the tract, roughly 1 mA per mm. These studies also show CST mapping can miss lateral fibers to the face and hand, a classic DTI weakness in the corticospinal fan.
- Therefore tractography complements, and does not replace, **direct electrical stimulation** and awake language mapping. These remain the gold standard.

Other applications: targeting the dentato-rubro-thalamic tract for tremor treated with deep brain stimulation or MR-guided focused ultrasound. Tract-based targeting may beat atlas coordinates, although trial data are still accumulating. Planning the medial forebrain bundle and subcallosal cingulate targets in depression DBS research (Riva-Posse) is another use. Laser ablation trajectories and epilepsy surgery, including protecting Meyer's loop, round out the list.

Open questions include automated, reproducible bundle segmentation (TractSeg and other deep-learning methods), harmonizing data across scanners, and achieving the sub-millimeter resolution of ultra-high-gradient Connectome scanners (300 mT/m) in routine practice. Validating microstructure models against histology also remains unresolved.

keyPoints: Diffusion MRI measures random water motion, which is anisotropic in white matter
DTI models each voxel as a tensor; FA ranges from 0 to 1
The principal eigenvector estimates fiber direction; color shows orientation
Tractography links directions into tracts, either deterministically or probabilistically
Crossing fibers, edema and false-positive bundles limit accuracy
Tractography guides resection near the CST, arcuate fasciculus and optic radiation, alongside direct stimulation

test.q: What physical process does diffusion MRI measure?
test.explain: Diffusion MRI detects the random (Brownian) motion of water molecules. Blood oxygenation is the basis of BOLD fMRI, not diffusion imaging.

test.q: Why is water diffusion anisotropic in white matter?
choices: Axon bundles hinder motion across fibers
Blood flow pushes water along vessels
test.explain: Parallel axonal membranes (and myelin) make water move more easily along the fibers than across them.

test.q: In the standard DTI color code, green represents fibers running:
test.explain: Red means left-right, green means anterior-posterior (front-back) and blue means superior-inferior (up-down).

test.q: What is the minimum number of gradient directions needed to estimate a diffusion tensor?
test.explain: A symmetric 3×3 tensor has six unknowns, so at least 6 directions plus a b=0 image are needed. Clinical protocols use 30 or more to improve accuracy.

test.q: Which tract is most often mapped to protect movement during tumor surgery?
test.explain: The corticospinal tract carries voluntary motor commands. The arcuate fasciculus serves language and the optic radiation serves vision.

test.q: What is the main weakness of a single-tensor model?
choices: It measures blood flow, not water
It blurs gray matter into white matter
It shows one fiber direction per voxel
test.explain: One tensor gives one principal direction, so voxels with crossing fibers are misrepresented.

test.q: How does probabilistic tractography differ from deterministic tractography?
choices: It samples a distribution of orientations
It steps along one fixed direction
It uses PET data instead of MRI
It runs without any seed region
test.explain: Probabilistic methods sample orientation uncertainty and output connection likelihood maps. Deterministic methods follow the single principal eigenvector.

test.q: Why can preoperative tract maps become inaccurate during surgery?
choices: Brain shift after the dura opens
The MRI magnet stays switched on
test.explain: Cerebrospinal fluid loss and resection move the brain, so preoperative tracts drift out of registration with the patient.

test.q: A bright DWI signal with low ADC classically indicates:
test.explain: Restricted diffusion (bright DWI, low ADC) is the hallmark of acute ischemia.

test.q: What is the name of the 0-to-1 index of how directional diffusion is in a voxel? (two words)
test.explain: FA is 0 for isotropic diffusion and approaches 1 for strongly directional diffusion.

test.q: Diffusion that is equal in all directions, as in cerebrospinal fluid, is called ___.
test.explain: Isotropic diffusion has no preferred direction. Anisotropic diffusion does.

test.q: The computer method that reconstructs 3D nerve pathways from diffusion data is called ___.
test.explain: Tractography links fiber directions from voxel to voxel to build tracts.

kidTest.q: What does the special scanner watch move inside the brain?
kidTest.explain: It watches how water jiggles and moves.

kidTest.q: Inside a wire bundle, water moves most easily:
kidTest.explain: Like cars on a highway, water zooms along the wire.

kidTest.q: What does the computer draw from the scan?
kidTest.explain: It draws lines showing where the brain's wire bundles go.

kidTest.q: Why do surgeons look at these maps?
kidTest.explain: They plan a path that keeps the wires for moving and talking safe.

kidTest.q: The brain's tiny message carriers are like electric w _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Nerve fibers are like wires that carry messages.

advancedTest.q: A tract seems to stop at the edge of a tumor surrounded by edema. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Edema raises FA and makes tracts look thicker
The tract has definitely been destroyed by the tumor
Low FA from edema may falsely halt tracking
The tumor reverses the direction of signal flow
advancedTest.explain: Edema lowers FA below the stopping threshold, causing false negatives. Constrained spherical deconvolution or free-water models can help recover the tract.

advancedTest.q: Anisotropy in non-myelinated garfish nerve implies that FA:
choices: Is a specific measure of myelin content
Is caused by artifacts in the scanner
Depends mainly on blood vessel orientation
advancedTest.explain: Beaulieu's finding shows that membranes alone create anisotropy, so FA is not a myelin-specific marker.

advancedTest.q: The ISMRM 2015 challenge showed tractography algorithms tend to:
choices: Reconstruct the bundles with high overall accuracy
Miss most true bundles but yield few false ones
Find most true bundles but add many false ones
Fail mainly in straight, isolated fiber tracts
advancedTest.explain: Sensitivity was good but specificity was poor, with many false-positive bundles at bottlenecks.

advancedTest.q: Why does direct electrical stimulation remain the gold standard over tractography?
choices: Stimulation measures the anisotropy of water directly
Tractography is rarely compatible with neuronavigation systems
Tractography renders tract width that depends on model thresholds
Stimulation produces higher-resolution images of the white matter
advancedTest.explain: Rendered tracts are model outputs that are sensitive to thresholds, crossings and brain shift. Stimulation tests real function during surgery.

lessons.title: PET Imaging: Radiotracers, Metabolism and Receptor Occupancy

levels.kid:
Imagine you want to know which rooms in a dark house are busy. You hand out tiny glowing marbles to everyone, and the busy rooms glow the most. That is a bit like a **PET scan**.

Doctors give a person a special sugar or medicine that carries a tiny, safe glowing tag. The brain grabs the tag where it is busy or where it fits into little locks on cells. The tag gives off tiny flashes. A ring-shaped camera catches the flashes and builds a picture.

PET helps doctors find a hidden tumor or spot where a seizure starts. Scientists also use it to see whether a medicine has reached its lock in the brain.
levels.hs:
**Positron emission tomography (PET)** makes images of chemistry in the living body. A **radiotracer** is a molecule tagged with a radioactive atom that decays by giving off a **positron**, the antimatter twin of an electron. After traveling about a millimeter, the positron meets an electron and both are destroyed. This **annihilation** releases two **gamma rays**, each with 511 keV of energy, flying in nearly opposite directions.

The PET scanner is a ring of detectors. When two detectors on opposite sides fire at almost the same moment (a **coincidence**), the computer knows the decay happened somewhere on the line between them. Millions of these lines are combined into a 3D map of where the tracer went.

Common tracer isotopes:
- **Fluorine-18**: half-life about 110 minutes
- **Carbon-11**: half-life about 20 minutes, so it must be made in an on-site cyclotron

The best-known tracer is **FDG** (fluorodeoxyglucose), a sugar look-alike. Busy brain cells take up more glucose, so FDG shows brain metabolism.

Real example: in a person with epilepsy that drugs cannot control, an FDG-PET scan between seizures often shows a region of *low* metabolism, frequently in a temporal lobe. Combined with EEG and MRI, this helps surgeons decide what tissue to remove.

PET is less sharp than MRI, but it measures molecules no other scanner can see.
levels.college:
PET quantifies the spatial and temporal distribution of a positron-emitting tracer given at **tracer doses**, amounts small enough not to perturb the biology being measured.

**Physics and image formation**
- Positron range blurs resolution. It is about 0.6 mm (mean) for F-18 and longer for C-11 and O-15.
- **Non-collinearity** blurs it further: the two photons are not exactly 180° apart.
- Clinical scanners reach about 4-5 mm resolution. **Time-of-flight** detection uses picosecond timing differences to localize events along each line, which improves signal-to-noise.
- Corrections for **attenuation** (from a CT or MR map), scatter and random coincidences are needed before quantification.

**FDG and metabolism**
FDG enters cells through GLUT transporters and is phosphorylated by **hexokinase** to FDG-6-phosphate. It cannot proceed down glycolysis, so it is **metabolically trapped**. Uptake therefore reflects the glucose metabolic rate. Much of brain glucose use supports synaptic activity, especially restoring ion gradients. Clinical uses include:
- Seizure focus localization (hypometabolism between seizures)
- Dementia patterns: temporoparietal and posterior cingulate loss in Alzheimer's; frontal and anterior temporal loss in frontotemporal dementia
- Tumor grading, though high normal cortical glucose uptake limits FDG for brain tumors. Amino-acid tracers such as **FET** are preferred.

**Receptor and pathology imaging**
- **[11C]raclopride**: D2/D3 dopamine receptors
- **[11C]PiB, florbetapir**: amyloid plaques
- **Flortaucipir**: tau tangles

The **standardized uptake value (SUV)** normalizes tissue activity to injected activity per body weight. It is simple but only semi-quantitative.

**Receptor occupancy**
Scan a subject at baseline and again after a drug. The drop in specific tracer binding shows the fraction of target receptors the drug occupies:

Occupancy = (BP_baseline − BP_drug) / BP_baseline

For example, antipsychotic studies linked D2 occupancy to both clinical response and side effects.
levels.phd:
Quantitative PET rests on **compartmental modeling**. A plasma **input function** drives exchange among tissue compartments: free plus nonspecifically bound tracer (C_ND) and specifically bound tracer (C_S). Rate constants K1-k4 describe delivery, efflux, binding and dissociation.

For FDG, the irreversible two-tissue model (k4 ≈ 0) gives the net influx constant Ki = K1k3/(k2+k3). Sokoloff's 2-deoxyglucose autoradiography method, adapted for FDG by Phelps, Reivich and colleagues around 1979, converts Ki to glucose metabolic rate using a **lumped constant**. This constant corrects for differences in how FDG and glucose are transported and phosphorylated. It is not universal, and it shifts in ischemia and tumors.

For reversible receptor ligands, the key outcome is **binding potential**. In the nomenclature consensus (Innis et al., 2007), BP_ND = f_ND·B_avail/K_D, the ratio of specific to nondisplaceable uptake at equilibrium. Arterial sampling is invasive. **Reference-tissue models** avoid it by using a region devoid of target as the input; for D2 receptors this is the cerebellum. The simplified reference tissue model (Lammertsma & Hume, 1996) and Logan graphical analysis are workhorses.

Occupancy rests on saturable, competitive binding: θ = BP reduction. Plotting occupancy against plasma drug concentration fits an E_max-type relation and yields an EC50 (in vivo potency).

Classic findings:
- **Farde and colleagues** (Karolinska) showed with [11C]raclopride that antipsychotic benefit tends to emerge around 65% striatal D2 occupancy. Extrapyramidal side effects rise above about 78-80%. Kapur's work refined this threshold model.
- **Endogenous competition**: raclopride binding falls after amphetamine-induced dopamine release (Laruelle; Breier). This allows indirect estimates of neurotransmitter release.

There is nuance here. The occupancy model mixes in receptor internalization and changes in affinity state, so the BP drop does not map linearly onto dopamine levels. High-affinity agonist radioligands (e.g., [11C]PHNO) are more sensitive to endogenous dopamine than antagonists. Low specific-to-nondisplaceable ratios, radiometabolites that cross the blood-brain barrier, and partial-volume effects in small structures all bias estimates.
levels.expert:
Modern **drug development** uses PET at the decision points that matter most. A Phase 0/I occupancy study answers three questions:
- Does the molecule cross the blood-brain barrier?
- Does it engage the target?
- What plasma exposure gives the intended occupancy?

This helps companies drop compounds that fail before costly efficacy trials. The "three pillars" framework (exposure at site, target binding, functional modulation) came from analyses of failed CNS programs that never confirmed target engagement. A related approach is **microdosing** with the radiolabeled drug itself to measure brain penetration directly. The limiting factor is often the lack of a validated radioligand for the target.

**Pitfalls practitioners watch for:**
- **Test-retest variability** of BP_ND (often 5-10%) limits detection of small occupancies.
- **Plasma-brain hysteresis**: occupancy may lag or outlast plasma levels, so timing relative to drug exposure matters.
- **Off-target binding**: first-generation tau tracers such as flortaucipir bind monoamine oxidase and neuromelanin, confounding the signal. This drove second-generation ligands (MK-6240, PI-2620).
- **TSPO** tracers for neuroinflammation are confounded by a common gene variant (rs6971). It splits people into high-, mixed- and low-affinity binders, so studies must genotype participants.

**Clinical neurology and neurosurgery:**
- Interictal FDG hypometabolism is often more extensive than the seizure onset zone. It is used to guide where stereo-EEG electrodes go, not to define resection margins alone.
- Amino-acid PET (FET, FDOPA, methionine) separates recurrent glioma from radiation necrosis and finds biopsy targets with high metabolic activity. RANO/PET guidelines formalize this.
- Amyloid PET is now central to deciding who is eligible for anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab). It is also used to document plaque clearance, with results reported in **Centiloid** units, a standardized scale that lets different amyloid tracers be compared.

**Advances and open questions:**
- Long axial field-of-view "total-body" scanners and PET/MR hybrids allow lower radiation, image-derived input functions and simultaneous functional MRI.
- Synaptic density imaging with [11C]UCB-J (targeting SV2A) offers an in vivo synapse count for epilepsy and neurodegeneration.
- It is unresolved how well PET occupancy predicts efficacy for targets without a clear occupancy-response threshold, such as allosteric modulators.

keyPoints: PET detects pairs of 511 keV gamma rays from positron annihilation
Radiotracers use isotopes like fluorine-18 (~110 min) and carbon-11 (~20 min)
FDG is trapped after hexokinase phosphorylation and maps glucose metabolism
Binding potential compares specific to nondisplaceable tracer binding
Receptor occupancy = drop in binding after a drug versus baseline
Antipsychotic benefit appears near 65% D2 occupancy; motor side effects rise near 80%

test.q: What does a PET scanner directly detect?
test.explain: A positron annihilates with an electron, releasing two 511 keV gamma rays in nearly opposite directions. Spinning protons describe MRI, not PET.

test.q: Why is FDG retained inside active cells?
choices: It is pumped in by sodium channels
It is stored as glycogen granules
test.explain: Hexokinase converts FDG to FDG-6-phosphate, which cannot continue through glycolysis, so it is metabolically trapped.

test.q: Why must carbon-11 tracers usually be made in an on-site cyclotron?
choices: They lose binding at room temperature
They are destroyed by the CT scan
They emit too little gamma energy
test.explain: Carbon-11 decays with a ~20-minute half-life, too fast to ship. Fluorine-18 (~110 minutes) can be transported.

test.q: Between seizures, FDG-PET in drug-resistant focal epilepsy often shows the focus as:
choices: A region of high glucose use
A region of raised blood flow
A region of bright amyloid signal
test.explain: Interictal scans typically show hypometabolism, often in a temporal lobe, which helps localize the seizure focus.

test.q: Which tracer is used to image D2/D3 dopamine receptors?
test.explain: [11C]raclopride binds D2/D3 receptors. Florbetapir images amyloid, flortaucipir images tau and FET images amino-acid uptake in tumors.

test.q: How is receptor occupancy by a drug measured with PET?
choices: Counting the drug molecules in a biopsy
Timing how fast the tracer reaches the brain
Comparing binding before and after the drug
Measuring blood oxygen changes during a task
test.explain: Occupancy equals the fractional drop in specific tracer binding after the drug compared with baseline.

test.q: Why is FDG less useful than amino-acid tracers for many brain tumors?
choices: FDG binds tightly to amyloid plaques
Tumors do not take up any glucose
FDG fails to cross the skull bone
Normal cortex already uses much glucose
test.explain: High background glucose metabolism in normal cortex hides tumor contrast, so tracers like FET are preferred.

test.q: Which regions typically show reduced FDG uptake in Alzheimer's disease?
choices: Primary motor and sensory cortex strips
test.explain: Alzheimer's disease classically reduces temporoparietal and posterior cingulate metabolism. Frontal and anterior temporal loss suggests frontotemporal dementia.

test.q: What does time-of-flight detection improve in PET?
choices: Removing the need for any radiotracer
test.explain: Picosecond timing differences between the two photons narrow where each event happened along its line, improving signal-to-noise.

test.q: What particle, the antimatter twin of an electron, does a PET isotope emit?
test.explain: Positron emitters such as F-18 and C-11 make PET possible.

test.q: The simple semi-quantitative PET measure normalizing activity to injected amount per body weight is the standardized ___ value.
test.explain: SUV stands for standardized uptake value.

test.q: What enzyme phosphorylates FDG inside cells?
test.explain: Hexokinase makes FDG-6-phosphate, which stays trapped in the cell.

kidTest.q: What does a PET scan camera catch?
choices: Tiny flashes from a special tag
kidTest.explain: The tag gives off tiny flashes that the ring camera catches.

kidTest.q: Which brain parts glow most on a sugar PET scan?
kidTest.explain: Busy cells use more sugar, so they take up more of the tagged sugar.

kidTest.q: What shape is the PET camera?
kidTest.explain: Detectors sit in a ring around the person.

kidTest.q: Why do scientists use PET with medicines?
choices: To change the color of the medicine
To see if a medicine reached its lock
To make the medicine taste sweeter
kidTest.explain: PET shows whether a medicine has reached its target in the brain.

kidTest.q: PET often uses a special tagged food the brain loves. It starts with s _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The tagged sugar called FDG shows which parts of the brain are busy.

advancedTest.q: Raclopride binding falls after amphetamine. The best explanation is:
choices: Released dopamine competes with the tracer at D2
Amphetamine destroys D2 receptors within minutes
Amphetamine blocks tracer transport into blood
Cerebellar binding rises and inflates the reference
advancedTest.explain: Endogenous dopamine released by amphetamine competes with raclopride, lowering BP_ND. Internalization adds nuance but does not mean receptor destruction.

advancedTest.q: Why is the cerebellum used as the reference region for D2 receptor studies?
choices: It shows the greatest occupancy by antipsychotics
It receives no blood flow, so tracer stays fixed
It has high D2 density for a strong signal
It has negligible D2 receptors, giving nondisplaceable uptake
advancedTest.explain: A reference region must lack the target so its uptake reflects only free plus nonspecific tracer, the comparison for specific binding.

advancedTest.q: A drug gives 90% striatal D2 occupancy. Based on PET work, what is most expected?
choices: Fewer side effects than drugs at 65% occupancy
Weak effect since benefit needs over 95%
Benefit with high extrapyramidal side-effect risk
No effect because occupancy is unrelated to response
advancedTest.explain: Benefit tends to start near 65%, while extrapyramidal effects rise above about 78-80%, so 90% raises side-effect risk.

advancedTest.q: Why must TSPO neuroinflammation PET studies genotype participants?
choices: Genotype sets the patient's positron range
A common variant (rs6971) alters tracer affinity
The gene controls the production of fluorine-18
The variant switches tracer to amyloid binding
advancedTest.explain: rs6971 splits people into high-, mixed- and low-affinity binders, so binding differences could reflect genotype rather than inflammation.
